_comment: Everything that is true of mathematics but NOT of every subject, in one place. A tree opts in with "subjectFamily": "mathematics" in its tree.json. Two halves, with different readers: `instructions` is spliced into the generated AI instructions by js/engine.js at runtime, and `decomposition` is read by a human or an agent following prompts/spec/decomposition.md when a new subject is authored. The engine ignores `decomposition` entirely. Duplication BETWEEN family files is deliberate and accepted: a teacher should be able to open one file and see the whole picture for their subject without chasing cross-references. This file carries its own `version`, cited separately from the instruction modules in the paper's appendix.
title: Mathematics

decomposition._comment: Read at authoring time, not by the engine: the builder appends every family's block to the authoring prompt, after prompts/decomposition.json (its `subjectFamilies` section tells the model so). Every key here that does not start with `_` is text the model reads.
decomposition.nodeTypeCharacter: In mathematics the skill/concept split is usually clean: a concept is a definition, a named quantity or a rule stated in words, and a skill is a procedure carried out on numbers or symbols. Where understanding a concept in practice demands extensive calculation before anyone would say it had been practised, that calculation does NOT belong in the concept node. Split it into its own skill node listing the concept among its prerequisites.
decomposition.skillVerbs: Name a skill node with a verb phrase for what the student does with numbers or symbols: "Calculate the growth factor from a percentage", "Draw the graph of a linear function", "Solve a quadratic equation by factorising". A noun-phrase name on a skill node is a sign the node needs reconsidering.
decomposition.loadBearingExamples: Load-bearing mathematical vocabulary that typically earns a node: coordinate system, term, factor, growth factor, function, variable. Ordinary words used in their everyday sense do not: "speed" in a sentence about a car earns no node, while "average speed" as a defined quantity does.
decomposition.prerequisiteDirection: Mathematics has unusually long prerequisite chains, and they are the whole point of the map. Be generous with dependencies WITHIN a topic, and check explicitly for the ones that cross topics (a statistics node depending on a fractions node, a geometry node depending on an algebra node) — these are the ones most often missed, and they are what makes the graph more than a list of topics.

add.text: The lead-in in this subject: instead of stating the rule, start with numbers. "Imagine multiplying 2 by itself 6 times: 2×2×2×2×2×2. That's tedious to write, so we write 2⁶ instead. We call this a power."
In this subject: no extensive calculation when testing a concept. If numbers appear, keep the calculation minimal.
In this subject, a [skill] point becomes a calculation problem and a [concept] point must not; if numbers appear in a [concept] task, keep the calculation minimal.

An example of the FORM of a starter (not its content): "Look at these fractions: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6, 1/8. Add some of them together to get as close to 1 as possible." Anyone can start, there is no single right answer, and students can keep going for minutes.

IN THIS SUBJECT the rounds above are the example–problem pair model, and you may call it that. The teacher's turn is one problem worked on the board with every step shown; the students' turn is the same kind of problem with different numbers or a new wrapping; the independent practice is three problem sets. Give a complete worked answer to every problem, not just the final number.
In this subject: keep calculation minimal in the blocks for a [concept] goal; the matching computational skill is a separate goal later in the tree.
The automaticity argument in this subject: if you know your times tables by heart, you don't spend effort on them, which leaves room for the hard and interesting part of the problem.

- Understanding numbers and percentages gives you control over your own money and agreements: you can see for yourself whether something is a good deal, such as what an insurance salesperson is really offering, or how to split costs fairly with the people you live with.
